Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit.

We represent: defendant.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that a court may consider documents incorporated by reference into the complaint on a Rule 12(b)(6) motion without converting it into a summary judgment motion.

Cite at least six decisions of the Ninth Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

answer:
## ARGUMENT

### The Court May Consider Documents Incorporated by Reference in the Complaint Without Converting Defendant's Rule 12(b)(6) Motion into One for Summary Judgment.

**A. Incorporated documents are properly before the Court on a motion to dismiss.**

Rule 12(d) requires conversion to summary judgment only when "matters outside the pleadings are presented to and not excluded by the court." Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(d). This Court has long held that documents incorporated by reference into the complaint are not "outside the pleadings." A court "may . . . consider certain materials—documents attached to the complaint, documents incorporated by reference in the complaint, or matters of judicial notice—without converting the motion to dismiss into a motion for summary judgment." *United States v. Ritchie*, 342 F.3d 903, 908 (9th Cir. 2003); *accord Coto Settlement v. Eisenberg*, 593 F.3d 1031, 1038 (9th Cir. 2010); *Daniels-Hall v. Nat'l Educ. Ass'n*, 629 F.3d 992, 998 (9th Cir. 2010).

The rule is not new. In *Branch v. Tunnell*, this Court held that a district court may consider documents "whose contents are alleged in a complaint and whose authenticity no party questions, but which are not physically attached to the [plaintiff's] pleading." 14 F.3d 449, 454 (9th Cir. 1994), *overruled on other grounds by Galbraith v. County of Santa Clara*, 307 F.3d 1119, 1127 (9th Cir. 2002); *see also In re Silicon Graphics Inc. Sec. Litig.*, 183 F.3d 970, 986 (9th Cir. 1999) (same), *abrogated on other grounds by South Ferry LP, No. 2 v. Killinger*, 542 F.3d 776, 784 (9th Cir. 2008).

**B. The doctrine applies where the complaint refers extensively to a document or the document forms the basis of the claim.**

A document is incorporated by reference "if the plaintiff refers extensively to the document or the document forms the basis of the plaintiff's claim." *Ritchie*, 342 F.3d at 908; *accord Marder v. Lopez*, 450 F.3d 445, 448 (9th Cir. 2006); *Khoja v. Orexigen Therapeutics, Inc.*, 899 F.3d 988, 1002 (9th Cir. 2018). The doctrine also reaches documents on which the plaintiff's claim "necessarily relies" even if the complaint does not quote them. It applies where "the plaintiff's claim depends on the contents of a document, the defendant attaches the document to its motion to dismiss, and the parties do not dispute the authenticity of the document, even though the plaintiff does not explicitly allege the contents of that document in the complaint." *Knievel v. ESPN*, 393 F.3d 1068, 1076 (9th Cir. 2005); *see also Davis v. HSBC Bank Nev., N.A.*, 691 F.3d 1152, 1160 (9th Cir. 2012) (considering documents incorporated by reference in the complaint on a motion to dismiss).

**C. The doctrine prevents a plaintiff from avoiding dismissal by selective pleading.**

The doctrine rests on a practical principle. It "prevents plaintiffs from selecting only portions of documents that support their claims, while omitting portions of those very documents that weaken—or doom—their claims." *Khoja*, 899 F.3d at 1002. A plaintiff cannot plead around the terms of the very document on which the claim depends and then insist that the Court ignore it. Consideration of the full document also gives effect to Rule 12(b)(6)'s purpose of testing the legal sufficiency of the claims actually pleaded. *See Knievel*, 393 F.3d at 1076.

**D. Consideration of the incorporated documents here requires no conversion.**

Each requirement is met. The Complaint [refers extensively to / relies on] [identify document(s)], and Plaintiff's claim[s] for [identify claim(s)] [depend on / are based on] their contents. *See Marder*, 450 F.3d at 448. Defendant has submitted true and complete copies of those documents as exhibits to its motion. Plaintiff cannot reasonably question their authenticity, because the Complaint itself invokes them. *See Branch*, 14 F.3d at 454; *Knievel*, 393 F.3d at 1076. Considering them is therefore consistent with Rule 12(d), and the motion need not be treated as one for summary judgment. *Ritchie*, 342 F.3d at 908.

Defendant also recognizes the limits on the doctrine. A court may not use an incorporated document to resolve factual disputes against a plaintiff's well-pleaded allegations. "[I]t is improper to assume the truth of an incorporated document if such assumptions only serve to dispute facts stated in a well-pleaded complaint." *Khoja*, 899 F.3d at 1003. Defendant does not ask the Court to do so. Defendant relies on the documents for what they say, namely their terms and contents, and not to contradict any well-pleaded fact. Because the Court can consider that undisputed content without crossing the line *Khoja* draws, the motion to dismiss should be decided under Rule 12(b)(6) on the complete record the Complaint itself places at issue.
